title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa definition
content: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder characterised by self-induced starvation, excessive weight loss, and distorted body image. It typically manifests during adolescence and predominantly affects females. It is the most common cause of admissions to child and adolescent psychiatric wards.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa epidemiology
content: Incidence: 37 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 20–30 years. Sex ratio: more common in females 5:1. Approximately 90% of patients are female. Prevalence is between 1:100 and 1:200.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa genetic and biological aetiology
content: Family studies indicate increased risk for first-degree relatives, suggesting a heritable component. Twin studies show higher concordance in monozygotic than dizygotic twins. Certain gene polymorphisms, particularly those involved in serotonin regulation and energy homeostasis, are associated with AN. Endocrine disturbances (hypercortisolaemia, altered leptin levels) and neuroimaging changes (reduced grey matter volume, altered reward system) have been observed.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa psychological and sociocultural aetiology
content: Psychological risk factors include perfectionism, rigidity, harm avoidance, low self-esteem, and obsessive-compulsive tendencies. Prior exposure to traumatic events or adverse childhood experiences is linked to AN. Sociocultural factors include cultural idealisation of thinness, peer and family pressure, media promoting thin ideals, and participation in activities emphasising leanness (e.g. ballet, gymnastics).

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa pathophysiology
content: Pathogenesis involves genetic predisposition (polygenic), neurobiological alterations (serotonin and dopamine dysregulation affecting mood and appetite; HPA axis hyperactivity causing hypercortisolaemia and amenorrhoea), psychological factors (perfectionism, cognitive inflexibility), and sociocultural pressures. Starvation induces neuroendocrine and metabolic changes that perpetuate the disorder in a vicious cycle.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa physical clinical features
content: Physical signs include reduced body mass index, bradycardia, hypotension, and enlarged salivary glands.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa physiological abnormalities
content: Physiological abnormalities include hypokalaemia, low FSH, LH, oestrogens and testosterone, raised cortisol and growth hormone, impaired glucose tolerance, hypercholesterolaemia, hypercarotinaemia, and low T3.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa DSM-5 diagnostic criteria
content: Diagnosis is based on DSM-5 criteria (BMI and amenorrhoea are no longer specifically mentioned): (1) Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements leading to significantly low body weight. (2) Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though underweight. (3) Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence on self-evaluation, or denial of the seriousness of the current low body weight.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa vs bulimia nervosa differential
content: Both AN and bulimia nervosa (BN) involve preoccupation with body weight/shape and abnormal eating behaviours. Unlike AN, BN is characterised by recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory behaviours (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, diuretics). Patients with BN typically maintain normal or slightly above-normal weight, whereas AN patients are significantly underweight.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa vs major depressive disorder differential
content: Both AN and MDD can present with weight loss, poor appetite, social withdrawal, and mood disturbances. In MDD, weight loss is unintentional and not associated with distorted body image or fear of weight gain. The primary focus in MDD is pervasive depressive mood and loss of interest, whereas in AN the primary focus is on weight and body image.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa vs hyperthyroidism differential
content: Both AN and hyperthyroidism can cause significant weight loss and increased physical activity. Hyperthyroidism is distinguished by increased heart rate, heat intolerance, and tremors, with elevated thyroid hormones on blood tests. In AN, thyroid function tests are typically normal or show low-normal function due to the body's adaptive response to starvation.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa management in adults
content: For adults with anorexia nervosa, NICE recommend considering one of: individual eating-disorder-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-ED), Maudsley Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults (MANTRA), or specialist supportive clinical management (SSCM).

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa management in children and young people
content: In children and young people, NICE recommend anorexia-focused family therapy as the first-line treatment. The second-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa cardiovascular complications
content: Cardiovascular complications include bradycardia, hypotension, and prolonged QT interval, increasing the risk of sudden cardiac death. Mitral valve prolapse may also occur.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa endocrine complications
content: Endocrine complications include amenorrhoea (due to hypothalamic dysfunction), thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism), growth hormone resistance, cortisol excess, and insulin resistance.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa gastrointestinal and bone complications
content: Gastrointestinal complications include gastroparesis, constipation, liver dysfunction, and superior mesenteric artery syndrome. Bone complications include osteopenia or osteoporosis due to decreased bone mineral density from low oestrogen levels.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa haematological and nutritional complications
content: Haematological complications include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anaemia. Nutritional deficiencies can lead to pellagra (niacin deficiency), scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), and Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency). Secondary complications from purging include electrolyte imbalances, dental issues, and Russell's sign (calluses on knuckles).

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa psychiatric complications
content: Patients with AN frequently have comorbid psychiatric conditions including depression, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and an increased risk of suicide.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa prognosis and mortality
content: AN has the highest mortality rate among psychiatric disorders. The standardised mortality ratio is approximately 5.86, meaning individuals with AN are almost six times more likely to die prematurely. Up to 10% of patients will eventually die because of the disorder. Most deaths occur due to complications from severe malnutrition or suicide.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa treatment outcomes
content: Approximately 50% of individuals with AN achieve full recovery, while around 20–30% remain chronically ill. The remaining patients may experience partial recovery but continue to struggle with body image issues or disordered eating. Early intervention improves outcomes significantly.

title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa definition
content: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by intentional compensatory behaviours such as self-induced vomiting, use of laxatives or diuretics, or excessive exercise.

title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa DSM-5 diagnostic criteria
content: DSM-5 criteria: (1) Recurrent binge eating (larger amount than most people would eat in similar circumstances). (2) Sense of lack of control during the episode. (3) Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, excessive exercise). (4) Binge eating and compensatory behaviours occur on average at least once a week for three months. (5) Self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape and weight. (6) Disturbance does not occur exclusively during episodes of anorexia nervosa.

title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa physical signs
content: Recurrent vomiting may lead to erosion of teeth and Russell's sign — calluses on the knuckles or back of the hand due to repeated self-induced vomiting.

title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa management in adults
content: Referral for specialist care is appropriate in all cases. NICE recommend bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help for adults as first-line. If unacceptable, contraindicated, or ineffective after 4 weeks, NICE recommend individual eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED). Pharmacological treatment: high-dose fluoxetine is currently licensed for bulimia, though long-term data is lacking.

title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa management in children
content: Children with bulimia nervosa should be offered bulimia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-BN).

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Definition and terminology
content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterised by qualitative impairment in social interaction and communication, and repetitive stereotyped behaviour, interests, and activities. DSM-5 uses the term 'autism spectrum disorder' (ASD); ICD-10 uses 'pervasive developmental disorder' (PDD). Symptoms are usually present during early childhood but may manifest later.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Genetic aetiology
content: Genetic causes including gene defects and chromosomal anomalies are seen in 25% of cases. Sibling recurrence risk is approximately 10%. Concordance in monozygotic twins is 36–60%. Advanced maternal age (≥40 years) and paternal age (≥50 years) are independently associated with ASD risk. Genetic diagnoses associated with ASD include tuberous sclerosis complex, fragile X syndrome, chromosome 15q11-13 duplication syndrome, Angelman syndrome, Rett's syndrome, and Down syndrome.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Immunisation and ASD
content: The available evidence does not support any association between immunisations and ASD.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Pathophysiology
content: The pathogenesis is not completely understood. Genetic, perinatal, and environmental factors may alter brain development. ASD may result from abnormal function in the hippocampal/amygdala regions and other brain areas. Altered cytokine levels affecting neuronal cell proliferation, neuron death, and synaptic pruning, as well as altered microglia affecting phagocytosis of neurons, may contribute.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – DSM-5 classification and severity levels
content: DSM-5 includes autism, Asperger's syndrome, and PDD-NOS under ASD. Severity is rated separately for social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviours: Level 1 (requiring support), Level 2 (requiring substantial support), Level 3 (requiring very substantial support).

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: social communication impairments
content: Children and adults with ASD show persistent deficits in social communication and interaction: failure to regulate social interaction with nonverbal cues (eye gaze, facial expression, gestures); failure to form and maintain appropriate relationships; social isolation; and deficits in social-emotional reciprocity. Symptoms are typically evident before 2–3 years of age.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: repetitive behaviours and associated features
content: Repetitive behaviours include stereotyped/repetitive motor mannerisms, inflexible adherence to nonfunctional routines or rituals, highly restricted fixated interests, and hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input. ASD is often associated with intellectual impairment or language impairment. ADHD (35%) and epilepsy (18%) are commonly seen in children with ASD. ASD is also associated with a higher head circumference to brain volume ratio.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – DSM-5 diagnostic criteria
content: DSM-5 diagnosis requires: (1) Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction across multiple contexts. (2) Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities (at least 2 of: stereotyped/repetitive movements; insistence on sameness; fixated interests; sensory hyper/hypo-reactivity). (3) Symptoms present in early developmental period. (4) Clinically significant functional impairment. (5) Not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Referral criteria (NICE 2011)
content: Refer children younger than 3 years if there is regression in language or social skills. Consider referring children and young people if concerned about possible ASD based on reported or observed signs/symptoms, factors associated with increased ASD prevalence, or the likelihood of an alternative diagnosis.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Differential diagnosis
content: ASD should be differentiated from: ADHD (social communication difficulties but normal pragmatic language, nonverbal behaviour, imaginative play; no restricted/repetitive patterns); social (pragmatic) communication disorder (impaired social communication but no restricted/repetitive behaviours); global developmental delay/intellectual disability (social responsiveness appropriate for developmental level); developmental language disorder (normal reciprocal social interactions and imaginative play).

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Multidisciplinary management and early intervention
content: Management requires multidisciplinary input from paediatricians, psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists, educational professionals, and social care workers. Early identification and intervention improve outcomes significantly. Core principles include structure, routine, and visual aids. Approaches include Applied Behaviour Analysis (ABA), TEACCH, and Early Intensive Behavioural Intervention (EIBI).

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Communication and social skills interventions
content: Speech and Language Therapy assists with language development and communicative function. The Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS) is a visual-based system for non-verbal or minimally verbal individuals. Social skills training provides structured teaching of social norms and behaviours. Occupational therapy includes sensory integration therapy and adaptive skills training.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Pharmacological management
content: No drug treats the core symptoms of ASD. For comorbid ADHD: methylphenidate, atomoxetine, or guanfacine may be used per NICE guidelines. For comorbid anxiety and OCD: SSRIs may have a role.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Transition to adult services
content: Transition planning begins in adolescence, focusing on life skills, further education, employment, and independent living. Many adults with ASD have coexisting mental health conditions requiring ongoing psychological and pharmacological interventions. Tailored vocational training and supported living environments may be necessary.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Definition
content: Bipolar disorder (formerly manic depression) is a chronic psychiatric condition characterised by severe mood swings ranging from depressive lows to manic highs. Two types are recognised: type I (mania and depression) and type II (hypomania and depression).

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Epidemiology
content: Incidence: 25 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 20–30 years. Sex ratio: 1:1. Typically develops in the late teen years. Lifetime prevalence: 2%.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Genetic aetiology
content: Family studies show higher prevalence among first-degree relatives. Monozygotic twin concordance is higher than dizygotic. GWAS have identified numerous susceptibility loci involving neurotransmission, ion channels, and intracellular signalling pathways. No single gene has been definitively implicated.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Environmental and psychosocial aetiology
content: Stressful life events (physical/emotional trauma, significant loss, substance misuse, medical conditions) can precipitate onset or trigger episodes. Prenatal and perinatal factors (maternal viral infections, delivery complications) increase risk. Personality traits (neuroticism, extraversion), negative cognitive styles, social isolation, and poor social support can contribute.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Pathophysiology: neurotransmitter dysregulation
content: During manic episodes, increased dopaminergic activity leads to heightened arousal and euphoria. Depressive episodes are associated with reduced serotonergic and noradrenergic transmission, resulting in low mood and anhedonia. Elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-6) have been detected during mood episodes.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Pathophysiology: neuroimaging and HPA axis
content: Neuroimaging shows reduced grey matter volume in prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, and abnormalities in the amygdala. Dysregulated prefrontal-limbic connectivity disrupts emotional homeostasis. The HPA axis shows hyperactivity with elevated cortisol during depressive states and blunted response during manic episodes. Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress further exacerbate cellular damage.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – DSM-5 classification
content: Bipolar I: at least one manic episode (lasting ≥7 days or any duration if hospitalisation required), may be preceded/followed by hypomanic or depressive episodes. Bipolar II: at least one hypomanic episode (≥4 consecutive days) and at least one major depressive episode, without full manic episodes. Cyclothymic disorder: numerous periods of hypomanic and depressive symptoms for ≥2 years (1 year in children), never without symptoms for >2 months.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – ICD-11 classification and specifiers
content: ICD-11: Bipolar type I (at least one manic episode with or without depressive episodes), Bipolar type II (at least one hypomanic and one depressive episode, no manic episodes), Cyclothymia (persistent mood instability ≥2 years). Specifiers include: anxious distress, mixed features, rapid cycling (≥4 episodes/year), psychotic features, seasonal pattern, peripartum onset.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Mania vs hypomania: key differences
content: Mania: severe functional impairment or psychotic symptoms (e.g. delusions of grandeur, auditory hallucinations) for 7 days or more; may require hospitalisation. Hypomania: decreased or increased function for 4 days or more; does not impair functional capacity; no psychotic symptoms; unlikely to require hospitalisation. The key differentiating feature from an exam perspective is the presence of psychotic symptoms, which indicates mania.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Mania/hypomania shared symptoms
content: Symptoms common to both mania and hypomania include: predominantly elevated or irritable mood; pressured speech; flight of ideas (rapid speech with frequent topic changes based on associations, distractions, or word play); poor attention; insomnia; loss of inhibitions (sexual promiscuity, overspending, risk-taking); increased appetite.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials: MDD (no manic/hypomanic episodes; absence of even one manic episode distinguishes from bipolar); borderline personality disorder (mood swings reactive to environmental factors, lasting hours not days/weeks); schizophrenia (persistent psychotic symptoms in absence of mood symptoms; psychotic features in bipolar are mood-congruent and occur during mood episodes).

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Pharmacotherapy: mood stabilisers
content: Lithium remains the mood stabiliser of choice for long-term management. Valproate and lamotrigine are alternatives, particularly if lithium is not tolerated or contraindicated. Atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, aripiprazole) can be used adjunctively for maintenance, especially with frequent relapses.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Management of acute mania
content: In acute mania, antipsychotics (e.g. olanzapine or haloperidol) or benzodiazepines may be required to manage agitation and psychotic symptoms. Antidepressants should be avoided due to the risk of triggering a manic episode. Consider stopping antidepressant if the patient is already taking one.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Management of depressive episodes
content: For depressive episodes in bipolar disorder, quetiapine or a combination of olanzapine and fluoxetine are recommended. If ineffective or not tolerated, lamotrigine may be considered. Fluoxetine is the antidepressant of choice when used. Talking therapies should also be addressed.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Psychological interventions
content: Psychological interventions specifically designed for bipolar disorder may be helpful. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) helps individuals understand their condition and develop coping strategies. Family-focused therapy provides education and improves communication. Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT) aims to stabilise daily routines and sleep patterns.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Primary care referral thresholds
content: If symptoms suggest hypomania, NICE recommend routine referral to the community mental health team (CMHT). If there are features of mania or severe depression, an urgent referral to the CMHT should be made.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Complications
content: Complications include: comorbid psychiatric disorders (anxiety, substance misuse, ADHD); significantly elevated suicide risk (15 times greater than general population); persistent cognitive deficits (memory, executive function, attention) even during euthymic periods; increased risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, and obesity; social and occupational dysfunction.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Prognosis
content: The course is typically chronic and relapsing. Approximately 60–70% of individuals with bipolar I disorder experience recurrence within five years. Rapid cycling (≥4 mood episodes per year) is associated with a more challenging prognosis. There is a 2–3 times increased risk of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and COPD. Non-adherence to treatment is associated with poorer prognosis.

title: Anxiety disorder: generalised – Definition
content: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is a common disorder. NICE define the central feature as 'excessive worry about a number of different events associated with heightened tension.'

title: Anxiety disorder: generalised – Epidemiology
content: Incidence: 2,000 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 40–50 years. Sex ratio: more common in females 2:1.

title: Anxiety disorder: generalised – Clinical features
content: Clinical features include: excessive and persistent worry about various events or activities, occurring more days than not for at least 6 months; difficulty controlling the worry; restlessness or feeling keyed up or on edge; fatigue; difficulty concentrating or mind going blank; irritability; muscle tension; sleep disturbance (difficulty falling or staying asleep, or restless, unsatisfying sleep); significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

title: Anxiety disorder: generalised – Differential diagnosis: physical causes
content: Always look for a potential physical cause when considering a psychiatric diagnosis. In anxiety disorders, important alternative causes include hyperthyroidism, cardiac disease, and medication-induced anxiety. Medications that may trigger anxiety include salbutamol, theophylline, corticosteroids, antidepressants, and caffeine.

title: Anxiety disorder: generalised – Stepwise management
content: NICE recommend a stepwise approach: Step 1: education about GAD and active monitoring. Step 2: low-intensity psychological interventions (individual non-facilitated self-help, individual guided self-help, or psychoeducational groups). Step 3: high-intensity psychological interventions (CBT or applied relaxation) or drug treatment. Step 4: highly specialist input (e.g. multi-agency teams).

title: Anxiety disorder: generalised – Drug treatment
content: NICE recommend sertraline as the first-line SSRI. If sertraline is ineffective, offer an alternative SSRI or SNRI (e.g. duloxetine, venlafaxine). If SSRIs/SNRIs are not tolerated, consider pregabalin. For patients under 30 years, warn of increased risk of suicidal thinking and self-harm; weekly follow-up is recommended for the first month.

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – Panic disorder epidemiology and risk factors
content: Panic disorder requires symptoms present for at least 1 month. Prevalence of panic attacks: 7–9%; prevalence of panic disorder: 1.5–2.5%. Twice as common in females. Two peaks of onset: ages 15–24 and 45–54. Risk factors include living alone, early parental loss, history of abuse, poor educational history, and urban living. 40% prevalence in first-degree relatives. Follows a chronic, mild, and stable course in 50% of patients.

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – Panic disorder management
content: Stepwise approach: Step 1: recognition and diagnosis. Step 2: treatment in primary care. Step 3: review and consideration of alternative treatments. Step 4: review and referral to specialist mental health services. Step 5: care in specialist mental health services. In primary care, NICE recommend either CBT or drug treatment. SSRIs are first-line. If contraindicated or no response after 12 weeks, imipramine or clomipramine should be offered.

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – OCD definition and epidemiology
content: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterised by the presence of obsessions (unwanted intrusive thoughts, images, or urges) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviours or mental acts the person feels driven to perform). Compulsions may be overt (observable) or covert (mental acts). Estimated prevalence: 1–3% of the population.

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – OCD risk factors
content: Risk factors for OCD include: family history; peak onset between 10–20 years; pregnancy/postnatal period; history of abuse, bullying, or neglect.

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – OCD management: mild functional impairment
content: For mild functional impairment: low-intensity psychological treatments including CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP). If insufficient or unable to engage in psychological therapy, offer a choice of either an SSRI or more intensive CBT (including ERP).

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – OCD management: moderate functional impairment
content: For moderate functional impairment: offer a choice of either an SSRI (any SSRI for OCD; fluoxetine specifically for body dysmorphic disorder) or more intensive CBT including ERP. Consider clomipramine as an alternative first-line drug if preferred, previously effective, or if SSRI is contraindicated.

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – OCD management: severe functional impairment
content: For severe functional impairment (e.g. >3 hours/day on obsessions/compulsions, severe interference/distress, very little control/resistance): refer to secondary care mental health team. Whilst awaiting assessment, offer combined SSRI and CBT (including ERP), or consider clomipramine as an alternative. If SSRI is effective, continue for at least 12 months to prevent relapse.

title: Anxiety, phobias, OCD – Exposure and response prevention (ERP)
content: ERP is a psychological method involving exposing the patient to an anxiety-provoking situation (e.g. dirty hands) and then preventing them from engaging in their usual safety behaviour (e.g. hand-washing). This helps them confront their anxiety; habituation leads to eventual extinction of the response. At least 12 weeks of treatment is required for an initial response.

title: Depression – Definition
content: Depression is a common mental health disorder characterised by persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, and loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities. It can also cause physical symptoms such as fatigue, changes in appetite, and sleep disturbances.

title: Depression – Epidemiology
content: Incidence: 1,000 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 40–50 years. Sex ratio: more common in females 2:1.

title: Depression – Biological aetiology
content: First-degree relatives of individuals with MDD have a 2–3 fold increased risk. Twin studies suggest heritability of 37–58%. Neurobiological factors include monoamine dysregulation (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine), HPA axis dysfunction with cortisol hypersecretion, structural/functional neuroimaging changes in prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, and reduced neuroplasticity/neurogenesis in the hippocampus. Chronic physical health conditions increase risk 2–3 fold.

title: Depression – Psychosocial and environmental aetiology
content: Psychosocial risk factors: adverse life events, childhood adversity (abuse, neglect, parental loss), chronic stressors, socioeconomic disadvantage (poverty, unemployment, housing insecurity), social isolation, negative thinking patterns, neuroticism, and poor coping strategies. Environmental factors: alcohol/drug misuse, medications (corticosteroids, beta-blockers, interferon), seasonal factors (SAD with onset in autumn/winter), and perinatal factors (hormonal fluctuations, psychosocial stressors).

title: Depression – Core clinical features
content: Core features: persistent low mood (sadness, emptiness, hopelessness most of the day, nearly every day); anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure in almost all activities); and decreased energy or increased fatigue. At least one of depressed mood or anhedonia must be present for diagnosis.

title: Depression – Additional clinical features
content: Additional features include: cognitive changes (difficulty concentrating, decision-making, excessive guilt, feelings of worthlessness); sleep disturbances (insomnia or hypersomnia); appetite changes (weight loss >5% in a month, or weight gain; decreased appetite in younger patients; increased appetite in atypical depression); psychomotor agitation or retardation; and recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

title: Depression – DSM-5 diagnostic criteria
content: Five or more of the following symptoms present during the same 2-week period (at least one must be depressed mood or anhedonia): depressed mood; markedly diminished interest/pleasure; significant weight loss/gain (>5% in a month) or appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia; psychomotor agitation or retardation; fatigue or loss of energy; feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt; diminished concentration or indecisiveness; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation. Symptoms must cause clinically significant distress/impairment, not be attributable to substances or medical conditions, and there must be no history of manic or hypomanic episodes.

title: Depression – Differential diagnosis
content: Psychiatric differentials: bipolar disorder (key to distinguish as antidepressants alone can precipitate mania); dysthymia/persistent depressive disorder (chronic, less severe); adjustment disorder with depressed mood (resolves within months of stressor); anxiety disorders (often coexist). Medical differentials: thyroid disorders (hypothyroidism mimics depression); neurological disorders (Parkinson's, MS); chronic pain; nutritional deficiencies (B12, folate, vitamin D); endocrine disorders (Cushing's, Addison's). Substance-induced: alcohol/drugs; medications (beta-blockers, corticosteroids, isotretinoin).

title: Depression – NICE 2022 severity classification
content: NICE (2022) uses a simplified classification: 'less severe' depression (encompasses subthreshold and mild depression; PHQ-9 score <16) and 'more severe' depression (encompasses moderate and severe depression; PHQ-9 score ≥16). Antidepressant medication should not be routinely offered as first-line treatment for less severe depression unless that is the patient's preference.

title: Depression – Management of less severe depression
content: NICE treatment options for less severe depression, in order of preference: guided self-help; group CBT; group behavioural activation (BA); individual CBT; individual BA; group exercise; group mindfulness and meditation; interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT); SSRIs; counselling; short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy (STPP). Shared decision-making and least intrusive treatment first are recommended.

title: Depression – Management of more severe depression
content: NICE treatment options for more severe depression, in order of preference: combination of individual CBT and antidepressant; individual CBT; individual BA; antidepressant medication (SSRI, SNRI, or another antidepressant based on history); individual problem-solving; counselling; STPP; IPT; guided self-help; group exercise.

title: Depression – Screening questions
content: Two questions used to screen for depression: 'During the last month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?' and 'During the last month, have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?' A 'yes' answer to either should prompt a more in-depth assessment.

title: Depression – Assessment tools: HAD scale and PHQ-9
content: Hospital Anxiety and Depression (HAD) scale: 14 questions (7 anxiety, 7 depression); each scored 0–3; score out of 21; severity: 0–7 normal, 8–10 borderline, 11+ case. PHQ-9: asks about the last 2 weeks; 9 items scored 0–3; includes self-harm items; <16 = less severe depression; ≥16 = more severe depression.

title: Depression – Depression vs dementia: distinguishing features
content: Features suggesting depression over dementia: short history and rapid onset; biological symptoms (weight loss, sleep disturbance); patient worried about poor memory; reluctant to take tests, disappointed with results; variable mini-mental test score; global memory loss (dementia characteristically causes recent memory loss).

title: Depression – Switching antidepressants (Maudsley guidelines)
content: Switching between citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline, or paroxetine to another SSRI: direct switch possible. Switching from fluoxetine to another SSRI: withdraw then leave a gap of 4–7 days before starting a low dose. Switching from SSRI to TCA: cross-tapering recommended (except fluoxetine: withdraw, leave 4–7 days, then start TCA at low dose). Switching from citalopram/escitalopram/sertraline/paroxetine to venlafaxine: direct switch possible (caution with paroxetine). Switching from fluoxetine to venlafaxine: withdraw then start venlafaxine at low dose 4–7 days later.

title: Depression – Seasonal affective disorder
content: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) describes depression occurring predominantly around the winter months, related to reduced exposure to natural light affecting circadian rhythms and melatonin regulation. SAD should be treated the same way as depression per NICE guidelines. Sleeping tablets should not be given as they can worsen symptoms. Evidence for light therapy is limited and it is not routinely recommended.

title: Anxiety disorder: post-traumatic stress disorder – Definition
content: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) can develop in people of any age following a traumatic event (e.g. major disaster, childhood sexual abuse, warfare, sexual assault, severe accidents). It encompasses what became known as 'shell shock' following the First World War. DSM-IV requires symptoms to be present for more than one month.

title: Anxiety disorder: post-traumatic stress disorder – Clinical features
content: Features include: re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares, repetitive and distressing intrusive images); avoidance (avoiding people, situations, or circumstances resembling the event); hyperarousal (hypervigilance for threat, exaggerated startle response, sleep problems, irritability, difficulty concentrating); emotional numbing (lack of ability to experience feelings, feeling detached from others); depression; drug or alcohol misuse; anger; and unexplained physical symptoms.

title: Anxiety disorder: post-traumatic stress disorder – Pathophysiology
content: Pathophysiology involves dysregulation of the HPA axis leading to abnormal cortisol levels, increased amygdala activity causing heightened fear responses, and decreased hippocampal volume contributing to memory impairments.

title: Anxiety disorder: post-traumatic stress disorder – Management
content: Following a traumatic event, single-session debriefing is not recommended. Watchful waiting may be used for mild symptoms lasting less than 4 weeks. Trauma-focused CBT or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy may be used in more severe cases. Drug treatment should not be used as routine first-line for adults. If drug treatment is used, venlafaxine or an SSRI (e.g. sertraline) should be tried. In severe cases, NICE recommends risperidone may be used.

title: Acute stress reaction – Definition
content: Acute stress disorder is defined as an acute stress reaction that occurs in the first 4 weeks after exposure to a traumatic event (threatened death, serious injury, e.g. road traffic accident, sexual assault). This is in contrast to PTSD, which is diagnosed after 4 weeks.

title: Acute stress reaction – Clinical features
content: Features include: intrusive thoughts (flashbacks, nightmares); dissociation (feeling 'in a daze', time slowing); negative mood; avoidance; and arousal (hypervigilance, sleep disturbance).

title: Acute stress reaction – Management
content: Trauma-focused CBT is usually used first-line. Benzodiazepines are sometimes used for acute symptoms (e.g. agitation, sleep disturbance) but should only be used with caution due to addictive potential and concerns that they may be detrimental to adaptation.

title: Schizophrenia – Definition
content: Schizophrenia is a chronic and severe mental disorder affecting approximately 1% of the global population. It is characterised by a wide range of cognitive, emotional, and behavioural symptoms. Hallmark symptoms are divided into positive (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech/behaviour), negative (social withdrawal, reduced emotional expression, anhedonia), and cognitive (impaired attention, memory, executive functioning) categories.

title: Schizophrenia – Epidemiology
content: Incidence: 16 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 30–40 years. Sex ratio: more common in males 1.4:1. Peak age of first-episode psychosis: approximately 15–30 years.

title: Schizophrenia – Genetic risk factors
content: The strongest risk factor is family history. Risk of developing schizophrenia: monozygotic twin has schizophrenia = 50%; parent has schizophrenia = 10–15%; sibling has schizophrenia = 10%; no relatives = 1%. Twin studies show MZ concordance of 40–50% vs DZ 10–15%. Susceptibility genes include DRD2, COMT, DAT1, and NRG1 variants.

title: Schizophrenia – Environmental and neurodevelopmental risk factors
content: Environmental risk factors: Black Caribbean ethnicity (RR 5.4); migration (RR 2.9); urban environment (RR 2.4); cannabis use (RR 1.4). Neurodevelopmental factors: prenatal complications (maternal infections, malnutrition, hypoxia, stress); obstetric complications (birth hypoxia, preterm birth); structural brain anomalies (reduced grey matter, ventricular enlargement, altered connectivity).

title: Schizophrenia – Schneider's first rank symptoms: auditory hallucinations and thought disorders
content: Schneider's first rank symptoms include auditory hallucinations of a specific type: two or more voices discussing the patient in the third person; thought echo; voices commenting on the patient's behaviour. Thought disorders (thought alienation): thought insertion; thought withdrawal; thought broadcasting.

title: Schizophrenia – Schneider's first rank symptoms: passivity phenomena and delusional perceptions
content: Passivity phenomena: bodily sensations being controlled by external influence; actions/impulses/feelings imposed on the individual or influenced by others. Delusional perceptions: a two-stage process where first a normal object is perceived, then there is a sudden intense delusional insight into the object's meaning (e.g. 'The traffic light is green therefore I am the King').

title: Schizophrenia – Other clinical features and negative symptoms
content: Other features include: impaired insight; incongruity/blunting of affect (inappropriate emotion for circumstances); decreased speech; neologisms (made-up words); catatonia. Negative symptoms: incongruity/blunting of affect; anhedonia (inability to derive pleasure); alogia (poverty of speech); avolition (poor motivation); social withdrawal.

title: Schizophrenia – ICD-10 classification
content: ICD-10 classifies schizophrenia as: F20.0 Paranoid (delusions and auditory hallucinations, relatively normal intellect and affect); F20.1 Hebephrenic (disorganised speech, behaviour, flat/inappropriate affect); F20.2 Catatonic (disturbances in movement); F20.3 Undifferentiated; F20.4 Post-schizophrenic depression; F20.5 Residual; F20.6 Simple (insidious negative symptoms, no history of psychotic episodes).

title: Schizophrenia – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials: bipolar disorder (psychotic symptoms are mood-congruent and occur during mood episodes; clear manic/hypomanic episodes distinguish it; cognitive impairment usually episodic); schizoaffective disorder (must have had a period of hallucinations/delusions without prominent mood symptoms; better psychosocial functioning than schizophrenia but worse prognosis than mood disorders); MDD with psychotic features (mood-congruent psychosis closely related to depressive themes; cognitive impairment less severe and improves with remission).

title: Schizophrenia – Management (NICE 2009)
content: Key NICE management points: oral atypical antipsychotics are first-line; CBT should be offered to all patients; close attention should be paid to cardiovascular risk-factor modification due to high rates of cardiovascular disease in schizophrenic patients (linked to antipsychotic medication and high smoking rates).

title: Schizophrenia – Prognostic factors
content: Favourable prognostic indicators: later age of onset; female gender; good premorbid functioning; higher educational attainment; acute onset with identifiable precipitants; predominance of positive symptoms; good treatment adherence; strong social support. Poor prognostic indicators: early age of onset (especially males); male gender; insidious onset; strong family history; gradual onset; low IQ; long prodromal phase; lack of obvious precipitant; prominent negative symptoms; cognitive impairment; poor treatment adherence; comorbid substance misuse; limited social support.

title: Schizophrenia – Long-term prognosis and outcomes
content: Approximately 20–30% of patients experience a relatively favourable outcome; about 50% demonstrate a moderate course with recurring episodes and partial remission; 20–30% experience a severe, chronic course. Life expectancy is reduced by approximately 15–20 years compared to the general population, primarily due to cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, respiratory conditions, and suicide. Suicide risk is significantly elevated: approximately 5–10% of patients die by suicide. Employment rates: 10–20% in competitive employment in the UK.

title: Dementias – Lewy body dementia definition
content: Lewy body dementia (LBD) is an increasingly recognised cause of dementia, accounting for up to 20% of cases. The characteristic pathological feature is alpha-synuclein cytoplasmic inclusions (Lewy bodies) in the substantia nigra, paralimbic, and neocortical areas. Up to 40% of patients with Alzheimer's disease also have Lewy bodies.

title: Dementias – Lewy body dementia epidemiology
content: Incidence: 60 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 70+ years. Sex ratio: 1:1. Relative incidence compared to Alzheimer's disease: Alzheimer's 5.00, LBD 1, Parkinson's disease 0.22, frontotemporal lobar degeneration 0.05, multiple system atrophy 0.01.

title: Dementias – Lewy body dementia pathophysiology
content: Abnormal accumulation of alpha-synuclein forms insoluble fibrils within neuronal cell bodies (Lewy bodies). This causes neurodegeneration through: direct toxicity (impaired mitochondrial function, oxidative stress); impaired proteostasis (ubiquitin-proteasome system impairment); and synaptic dysfunction (impaired vesicle trafficking and neurotransmitter release). Cognitive impairment results from cortical neurodegeneration; parkinsonism from substantia nigra involvement; visual hallucinations from occipital cortex involvement; autonomic dysfunction from peripheral autonomic nervous system involvement.

title: Dementias – Lewy body dementia clinical features
content: Features include: progressive cognitive impairment (early impairments in attention and executive function rather than just memory loss, in contrast to Alzheimer's); fluctuating cognition (in contrast to other dementias); parkinsonism (usually develops after cognitive impairment); visual hallucinations (delusions and non-visual hallucinations may also be seen).

title: Dementias – Lewy body dementia investigations
content: Diagnosis is usually clinical. SPECT (single-photon emission computed tomography), commercially known as DaTscan, is increasingly used. The radioisotope used is dopaminergic iodine-123-radiolabelled 2-carbomethoxy-3-(4-iodophenyl)-N-(3-fluoropropyl) nortropane (123-I FP-CIT). Sensitivity of SPECT in diagnosing LBD is approximately 90% with a specificity of 100%.

title: Dementias – Lewy body dementia management
content: Both acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. donepezil, rivastigmine) and memantine can be used, as in Alzheimer's disease. Neuroleptics (antipsychotics) should be avoided in LBD as patients are extremely sensitive and may develop irreversible parkinsonism.

title: Wernicke's encephalopathy – Korsakoff's syndrome overview
content: Korsakoff's syndrome is a marked memory disorder often seen in alcoholics. Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency causes damage and haemorrhage to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus and the medial thalamus. It often follows on from untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy.

title: Wernicke's encephalopathy – Korsakoff's syndrome features
content: Features of Korsakoff's syndrome include: anterograde amnesia (inability to acquire new memories); retrograde amnesia; and confabulation (fabrication of memories to fill gaps).

title: Substance use disorder – Alcohol: safe drinking guidelines
content: The Chief Medical Officer (2016) recommends that both men and women should drink no more than 14 units of alcohol per week, spread evenly over 3 or more days. Pregnant women should not drink alcohol at all. One unit of alcohol = 10 mL of pure ethanol. Examples: 25 ml spirits (40% ABV) = 1 unit; one-third pint of beer (5–6% ABV) = 1 unit; half a 175 ml glass of red wine (12% ABV) = approximately 1 unit.

title: Substance use disorder – Alcohol withdrawal mechanism
content: Chronic alcohol consumption enhances GABA-mediated inhibition in the CNS and inhibits NMDA-type glutamate receptors. Alcohol withdrawal leads to the opposite: decreased inhibitory GABA and increased NMDA glutamate transmission, resulting in CNS excitability.

title: Substance use disorder – Alcohol withdrawal clinical features and timeline
content: Symptoms start at 6–12 hours: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety. Peak incidence of seizures at 36 hours. Peak incidence of delirium tremens at 48–72 hours: features include coarse tremor, confusion, delusions, auditory and visual hallucinations, fever, and tachycardia.

title: Substance use disorder – Alcohol withdrawal management
content: Patients with a history of complex withdrawals (delirium tremens, seizures, blackouts) should be admitted to hospital. First-line: long-acting benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide or diazepam) given as a reducing dose protocol. Lorazepam is preferred in patients with hepatic failure/cirrhosis (metabolised via glucuronidation, less affected by liver function). Chlordiazepoxide undergoes hepatic oxidation via CYP450, which is impaired in cirrhosis. Carbamazepine is also effective. Phenytoin is not effective for alcohol withdrawal seizures.

title: Substance use disorder – Alcohol: pharmacological treatments for dependence
content: Disulfiram promotes abstinence by inhibiting acetaldehyde dehydrogenase; even small amounts of alcohol (in perfumes, foods, mouthwashes) cause severe reactions. Contraindications: ischaemic heart disease and psychosis. Acamprosate reduces craving; it is a weak NMDA receptor antagonist and improves abstinence in placebo-controlled trials. SIGN recommends oral thiamine for alcoholic patients whose diet may be deficient.

title: Schizophrenia – Typical antipsychotics: mechanism and examples
content: Typical antipsychotics act as dopamine D2 receptor antagonists, blocking dopaminergic transmission in the mesolimbic pathways. Examples include haloperidol and chlorpromazine. They are associated with extrapyramidal side-effects and hyperprolactinaemia.

title: Schizophrenia – Typical antipsychotics: extrapyramidal side-effects
content: Extrapyramidal side-effects (EPSEs) include: parkinsonism; acute dystonia (sustained muscle contraction, e.g. torticollis, oculogyric crisis) — managed with procyclidine; akathisia (severe restlessness); and tardive dyskinesia (late-onset choreoathetoid movements, abnormal involuntary movements occurring in up to 40% of patients, may be irreversible, most commonly chewing and pouting of the jaw).

title: Schizophrenia – Typical antipsychotics: other side-effects
content: Other side-effects include: antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation); sedation; weight gain; raised prolactin (may cause galactorrhoea due to inhibition of the dopaminergic tuberoinfundibular pathway); impaired glucose tolerance; neuroleptic malignant syndrome (pyrexia, muscle stiffness); reduced seizure threshold; and prolonged QT interval (particularly haloperidol). MHRA warnings for elderly patients: increased risk of stroke and venous thromboembolism.

title: Schizophrenia – Atypical antipsychotics: first-line recommendation and mechanism
content: Atypical antipsychotics should be used first-line in patients with schizophrenia (NICE 2005). They act on a variety of receptors (D2, D3, D4, 5-HT). The main advantage over typical antipsychotics is a significant reduction in extrapyramidal side-effects.

title: Schizophrenia – Atypical antipsychotics: adverse effects and examples
content: Adverse effects include weight gain, hyperprolactinaemia, and metabolic effects. Clozapine is associated with agranulocytosis. MHRA warnings for elderly: increased risk of stroke and VTE. Examples: clozapine; olanzapine (higher risk of dyslipidaemia and obesity); risperidone; quetiapine; amisulpride; aripiprazole (generally good side-effect profile, particularly for prolactin elevation).

title: Schizophrenia – Antipsychotic monitoring requirements
content: Monitoring requirements: FBC, U&E, LFT — at start of therapy and annually (clozapine requires much more frequent FBC monitoring, initially weekly). Lipids and weight — at start, at 3 months, and annually. Fasting blood glucose and prolactin — at start, at 6 months, and annually. Blood pressure — baseline and frequently during dose titration. ECG — baseline. Cardiovascular risk assessment — annually.

title: Schizophrenia – Clozapine: indication and criteria
content: Clozapine should only be used in patients resistant to other antipsychotic medication. It should be introduced if schizophrenia is not controlled despite the sequential use of two or more antipsychotic drugs (one of which should be a second-generation antipsychotic drug), each for at least 6–8 weeks.

title: Schizophrenia – Clozapine: adverse effects and monitoring
content: Adverse effects: agranulocytosis (1%), neutropaenia (3%), reduced seizure threshold (seizures in up to 3% of patients), constipation, myocarditis (baseline ECG required before starting), and hypersalivation. FBC monitoring is essential — initially weekly. Dose adjustment may be necessary if smoking is started or stopped during treatment.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Lithium: uses and pharmacokinetics
content: Lithium is a mood-stabilising drug used most commonly prophylactically in bipolar disorder and as an adjunct in refractory depression. It has a very narrow therapeutic range (0.4–1.0 mmol/L) and a long plasma half-life, being excreted primarily by the kidneys.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Lithium: mechanism of action
content: The mechanism of action is not fully understood. Two theories: (1) interferes with inositol triphosphate formation; (2) interferes with cAMP formation.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Lithium: adverse effects
content: Adverse effects include: nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea; fine tremor; nephrotoxicity (polyuria, secondary to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus); thyroid enlargement (may lead to hypothyroidism); ECG changes (T-wave flattening/inversion); weight gain; idiopathic intracranial hypertension; leucocytosis; and hyperparathyroidism with resultant hypercalcaemia.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Lithium: monitoring protocol
content: When checking lithium levels, the sample should be taken 12 hours post-dose. After starting lithium, levels should be performed weekly and after each dose change until concentrations are stable. Once established, lithium blood levels should normally be checked every 3 months. After a dose change, levels should be taken a week later and weekly until stable. Thyroid and renal function should be checked every 6 months. Patients should be issued with an information booklet, alert card, and record book.

title: Depression – SSRIs: first-line use and preferred agents
content: SSRIs are considered first-line treatment for the majority of patients with depression. Citalopram and fluoxetine are currently the preferred SSRIs. Sertraline is useful post-myocardial infarction as there is more evidence for its safe use in this situation. SSRIs should be used with caution in children and adolescents; fluoxetine is the drug of choice when an antidepressant is indicated.

title: Depression – SSRIs: adverse effects
content: Adverse effects: gastrointestinal symptoms are the most common side-effect; increased risk of GI bleeding with NSAIDs (co-prescribe PPI); hyponatraemia; patients should be counselled about increased anxiety and agitation after starting an SSRI; fluoxetine and paroxetine have a higher propensity for drug interactions.

title: Depression – Citalopram and QT interval (MHRA 2011 warning)
content: Citalopram and escitalopram are associated with dose-dependent QT interval prolongation and should not be used in those with congenital long QT syndrome, known pre-existing QT interval prolongation, or in combination with other medicines that prolong the QT interval. Maximum daily dose: 40 mg for adults; 20 mg for patients older than 65 years; 20 mg for those with hepatic impairment.

title: Depression – SSRIs: drug interactions
content: Key interactions: NSAIDs (NICE advise 'do not normally offer SSRIs'; if given, co-prescribe PPI); warfarin/heparin (NICE recommend avoiding SSRIs and considering mirtazapine); triptans (avoid SSRIs — increased risk of serotonin syndrome); MAOIs (increased risk of serotonin syndrome).

title: Depression – SSRIs: follow-up, stopping, and discontinuation symptoms
content: After initiating antidepressant therapy, review at 2 weeks (under 25 years or high suicide risk: review at 1 week). Continue treatment for at least 6 months after remission to reduce relapse risk. When stopping, gradually reduce dose over 4 weeks (not necessary with fluoxetine). Paroxetine has a higher incidence of discontinuation symptoms. Discontinuation symptoms: increased mood change, restlessness, difficulty sleeping, unsteadiness, sweating, GI symptoms (pain, cramping, diarrhoea, vomiting), paraesthesia.

title: Depression – SSRIs in pregnancy
content: Use during the first trimester gives a small increased risk of congenital heart defects. Use during the third trimester can result in persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Paroxetine has an increased risk of congenital malformations, particularly in the first trimester. The BNF advises weighing up benefits and risks when deciding whether to use SSRIs in pregnancy.

title: Depression – Tricyclic antidepressants: mechanism and indications
content: TCAs inhibit the reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) and noradrenaline (NA), increasing their synaptic cleft concentrations. They are used less commonly for depression due to side-effects and toxicity in overdose, but are widely used for neuropathic pain (at smaller doses). Low-dose amitriptyline is used for neuropathic pain and prophylaxis of headache (tension and migraine).

title: Depression – Tricyclic antidepressants: side-effects
content: Side-effects include: antihistamine effects (drowsiness); antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention); adrenergic antagonism (postural hypotension); and QT interval prolongation.

title: Depression – Tricyclic antidepressants: overdose risk and drug choice
content: Lofepramine has a lower incidence of toxicity in overdose. Amitriptyline and dosulepin (dothiepin) are considered the most dangerous in overdose. More sedative TCAs: amitriptyline, clomipramine, dosulepin, trazodone. Less sedative: imipramine, lofepramine, nortriptyline.

title: Depression – MAOIs: overview and indications
content: Serotonin and noradrenaline are metabolised by monoamine oxidase in the presynaptic cell. Non-selective MAOIs (e.g. tranylcypromine, phenelzine) are used in the treatment of atypical depression (e.g. hyperphagia) and other psychiatric disorders, but are not used frequently due to side-effects.

title: Depression – MAOIs: adverse effects and tyramine interactions
content: Adverse effects include hypertensive reactions with tyramine-containing foods (cheese, pickled herring, Bovril, Oxo, Marmite, broad beans) and anticholinergic effects. Patients must be warned to avoid tyramine-containing foods.

title: Depression – Mirtazapine: mechanism and clinical use
content: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant that works by blocking alpha2-adrenergic receptors, which increases the release of neurotransmitters. It has fewer side-effects and interactions than many other antidepressants, making it useful in older people. Side-effects of sedation and increased appetite can be beneficial in older patients with insomnia and poor appetite. It is generally taken in the evening due to its sedative effect.

title: Depression – SNRIs: mechanism and indications
content: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) inhibit the reuptake of both serotonin and noradrenaline, increasing their concentrations in the synaptic cleft. Examples include venlafaxine and duloxetine. They are used to treat major depressive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and menopausal symptoms.

title: Substance use disorder – Benzodiazepines: mechanism and uses
content: Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening. They are used for: sedation, hypnotic, anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, and muscle relaxant purposes. Barbiturates, by contrast, increase the duration of chloride channel opening.

title: Substance use disorder – Benzodiazepines: dependence and withdrawal protocol
content: Patients commonly develop tolerance and dependence. The Committee on Safety of Medicines advises prescribing for a short period only (2–4 weeks). Withdrawal protocol (BNF): switch to equivalent dose of diazepam; reduce by approximately 1/8 (range 1/10–1/4) of daily dose every fortnight; steps of 2–2.5 mg every 2–3 weeks; withdrawal may take 4 weeks to over a year.

title: Substance use disorder – Benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome
content: Benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome is very similar to alcohol withdrawal syndrome and may occur up to 3 weeks after stopping a long-acting drug. Features include: insomnia; irritability; anxiety; tremor; loss of appetite; tinnitus; perspiration; perceptual disturbances; and seizures.

title: Substance use disorder – Z drugs: mechanism and types
content: Z drugs have similar effects to benzodiazepines but are structurally different. They act on the α2-subunit of the GABA receptor. Three groups: imidazopyridines (e.g. zolpidem); cyclopyrrolones (e.g. zopiclone); pyrazolopyrimidines (e.g. zaleplon). Adverse effects are similar to benzodiazepines; they increase the risk of falls in the elderly.

title: Depression – Insomnia: definition and classification
content: Insomnia is defined (DSM-V) as difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early-morning awakening leading to dissatisfaction with sleep quality, despite adequate time and opportunity for sleep, resulting in impaired daytime functioning. Acute insomnia is typically related to a life event and resolves without treatment. Chronic insomnia: trouble sleeping at least 3 nights per week for 3 months or longer.

title: Depression – Insomnia: risk factors
content: Risk factors include: female gender; increased age; lower educational attainment; unemployment; economic inactivity; widowed, divorced, or separated status; alcohol and substance abuse; stimulant usage; medications (e.g. corticosteroids); poor sleep hygiene; chronic pain; chronic illness (diabetes, CAD, hypertension, heart failure, BPH, COPD); psychiatric illness (anxiety, depression, mania, PTSD).

title: Depression – Insomnia: management
content: Identify potential causes. Advise not to drive while sleepy. Advise good sleep hygiene (no screens before bed, limited caffeine, fixed bed times). Only consider hypnotics if daytime impairment is severe. Recommended hypnotics: short-acting benzodiazepines or Z-drugs (zopiclone, zolpidem, zaleplon). Diazepam not recommended (useful only if insomnia linked to daytime anxiety). Use lowest effective dose for shortest period. Do not prescribe another hypnotic if no response to first. Review after 2 weeks; consider CBT referral.

title: Depression – Electroconvulsive therapy: indications and contraindications
content: ECT is a useful treatment option for patients with severe depression refractory to medication, catatonia, and those with psychotic symptoms. The only absolute contraindication is raised intracranial pressure.

title: Depression – Electroconvulsive therapy: side-effects
content: Short-term side-effects: headache; nausea; short-term memory impairment; memory loss of events prior to ECT; cardiac arrhythmia. Long-term side-effects: some patients report impaired memory.

title: Personality disorder – Definition and prevalence
content: Personality disorders (PD) are a group of mental health conditions characterised by persistent patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving that are significantly different from cultural expectations, leading to distress or problems in personal, social, and occupational functioning. Approximately 1 in 20 people have a personality disorder.

title: Personality disorder – ICD-11 classification: severity and trait domains
content: ICD-11 uses a dimensional model based on severity (mild, moderate, severe) and trait domains. Trait domains include: Negative Affectivity (wide range of negative emotions, mood swings); Detachment (avoidance of social interactions, emotional withdrawal); Dissociality (disregard for rights of others, lack of empathy); Disinhibition (impulsiveness, risk-taking); Anankastia (preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism); and Borderline Pattern (emotional instability, unstable relationships, fluctuating identity, impulsivity).

title: Personality disorder – Cluster A: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal features
content: Cluster A ('Odd or Eccentric'): Paranoid (hypersensitivity, unwarranted questioning of loyalty, reluctance to confide, conspirational beliefs, unwarranted perception of attacks). Schizoid (indifference to praise/criticism, preference for solitary activities, lack of interest in sex, emotional coldness, few friends). Schizotypal (ideas of reference, odd beliefs and magical thinking, unusual perceptual disturbances, paranoid ideation, odd eccentric behaviour, inappropriate affect, odd speech).

title: Personality disorder – Cluster B: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic features
content: Cluster B ('Dramatic, Emotional, or Erratic'): Antisocial (failure to conform to social norms, deception, impulsiveness, irritability/aggressiveness, reckless disregard for safety, irresponsibility, lack of remorse; more common in men). Borderline/Emotionally Unstable (efforts to avoid abandonment, unstable relationships, unstable self-image, impulsivity, recurrent suicidal behaviour, affective instability, chronic emptiness, difficulty controlling temper, quasi-psychotic thoughts). Histrionic (inappropriate sexual seductiveness, need to be centre of attention, rapidly shifting shallow emotions, suggestibility, self-dramatisation). Narcissistic (grandiose sense of self-importance, sense of entitlement, lack of empathy, excessive need for admiration, chronic envy).

title: Personality disorder – Cluster C: obsessive-compulsive, avoidant, dependent features
content: Cluster C ('Anxious and Fearful'): Obsessive-compulsive (preoccupation with details/rules/order, perfectionism hampering task completion, extreme dedication to work, rigid morality, inability to discard things, unwillingness to delegate, stingy spending). Avoidant (avoidance of occupational activities due to fear of criticism/rejection, unwillingness to be involved unless certain of being liked, social isolation with craving for social contact, views self as inept/inferior). Dependent (difficulty making decisions without reassurance, need for others to assume responsibility, difficulty expressing disagreement, lack of initiative, unrealistic fears of being left alone).

title: Personality disorder – Management
content: Personality disorders are difficult to treat. Approaches shown to help include: psychological therapies (dialectical behaviour therapy is particularly used for borderline personality disorder) and treatment of any coexisting psychiatric conditions.

title: Schizophrenia – Psychosis: definition and features
content: Psychosis describes a person experiencing things differently from those around them. Psychotic features include: hallucinations (e.g. auditory); delusions; thought disorganisation; alogia (little information conveyed by speech); tangentiality (answers diverge from topic); clanging; and word salad (linking real words incoherently into nonsensical content). Associated features: agitation/aggression; neurocognitive impairment; depression; thoughts of self-harm.

title: Schizophrenia – Conditions causing psychosis
content: Psychotic symptoms may occur in: schizophrenia (most common psychotic disorder); depression (psychotic depression, more common in elderly); bipolar disorder; puerperal psychosis; brief psychotic disorder (symptoms <1 month); neurological conditions (Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease); prescribed drugs (e.g. corticosteroids); and certain illicit drugs (e.g. cannabis, phencyclidine).

title: Schizophrenia – Thought disorders: definitions
content: Circumstantiality: inability to answer a question without excessive unnecessary detail, but eventually returns to the original point. Tangentiality: wandering from a topic without returning to it. Neologisms: new word formations, including combining two words. Clang associations: ideas related only by the fact they sound similar or rhyme. Word salad: completely incoherent speech with real words strung together into nonsense sentences. Knight's move thinking: severe loosening of associations with unexpected illogical leaps from one idea to another (feature of schizophrenia). Flight of ideas: leaps from one topic to another with discernible links (feature of mania). Perseveration: repetition of ideas or words despite attempts to change the topic. Echolalia: repetition of someone else's speech including the question asked.

title: Dementias – Charles-Bonnet syndrome: definition
content: Charles-Bonnet syndrome (CBS) is characterised by persistent or recurrent complex hallucinations (usually visual or auditory), occurring in clear consciousness, generally against a background of visual impairment (though visual impairment is not mandatory). Insight is usually preserved. This must occur in the absence of any other significant neuropsychiatric disturbance.

title: Dementias – Charles-Bonnet syndrome: epidemiology and risk factors
content: Incidence: 100 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 70+ years. Sex ratio: 1:1. No familial predisposition. Risk factors: advanced age; peripheral visual impairment; social isolation; sensory deprivation; early cognitive impairment. Most common associated ophthalmological conditions: age-related macular degeneration, followed by glaucoma and cataract.

title: Dementias – Charles-Bonnet syndrome: clinical features and prognosis
content: Well-formed complex visual hallucinations occur in 10–30% of individuals with severe visual impairment. Prevalence of CBS in visually impaired people is 11–15%. Around one-third find the hallucinations unpleasant or disturbing. In a large study, 88% had CBS for 2 years or more, resolving in only 25% at 9 years — it is not generally a transient experience.

title: Depression – Grief reaction: normal stages
content: Normal grief reaction involves 5 stages: (1) Denial (may include numbness and pseudohallucinations of the deceased — both auditory and visual; focus on physical objects or preparing meals for the deceased). (2) Anger (commonly directed at family members and medical professionals). (3) Bargaining. (4) Depression. (5) Acceptance. Many patients will not go through all 5 stages.

title: Depression – Grief reaction: abnormal grief
content: Abnormal (atypical) grief reactions are more likely in women and if the death is sudden and unexpected. Other risk factors: problematic relationship before death; poor social support. Features: delayed grief (sometimes defined as >2 weeks before grieving begins); prolonged grief (difficult to define; normal grief reactions may take up to and beyond 12 months).

title: Schizophrenia – Pseudohallucinations: definition and clinical relevance
content: A pseudohallucination is a false sensory perception in the absence of external stimuli when the affected person is aware that they are hallucinating. There is no mention of pseudohallucinations in ICD-10 or DSM-5. An example is a hypnagogic hallucination (vivid auditory or visual hallucination occurring when transitioning from wakefulness to sleep). Pseudohallucinations commonly occur in people who are grieving. Patients may need reassurance that these experiences are normal and do not indicate mental illness.

title: Depression – Cotard syndrome
content: Cotard syndrome is a rare mental disorder where the affected patient believes that they (or in some cases just a part of their body) is either dead or non-existent. This delusion is often difficult to treat and can result in significant problems as patients may stop eating or drinking. Cotard syndrome is associated with severe depression and psychotic disorders.

title: Personality disorder – De Clerambault's syndrome (erotomania)
content: De Clerambault's syndrome, also known as erotomania, is a form of paranoid delusion with an amorous quality. The patient (often a single woman) believes that a famous person is in love with her.

title: Personality disorder – Othello's syndrome (pathological jealousy)
content: Othello's syndrome is pathological jealousy where a person is convinced their partner is cheating on them without any real proof. This is accompanied by socially unacceptable behaviour linked to these claims.

title: Schizophrenia – Delusional parasitosis
content: Delusional parasitosis is a relatively rare condition where a patient has a fixed, false belief (delusion) that they are infested by 'bugs' (e.g. worms, parasites, mites, bacteria, fungus). It may occur in conjunction with other psychiatric conditions or may present alone, with patients often otherwise quite functional despite the delusion.

title: Dementias – Post-concussion syndrome
content: Post-concussion syndrome is seen after even minor head trauma. Typical features include headache, fatigue, anxiety/depression, and dizziness.

title: Depression – Sleep paralysis: definition and management
content: Sleep paralysis is a common condition characterised by transient paralysis of skeletal muscles occurring when awakening from sleep or less often while falling asleep. It is thought to be related to the paralysis that occurs as a natural part of REM sleep. Features: paralysis after waking or before falling asleep; hallucinations (images or speaking during the paralysis). Management: if troublesome, clonazepam may be used.

title: Schizophrenia – Mental Health Act: Section 2
content: Section 2 is used for admission for assessment for up to 28 days; it is not renewable. An Approved Mental Health Professional (AMHP) or rarely the nearest relative (NR) makes the application on the recommendation of 2 doctors, one of whom should be approved under Section 12(2) of the Mental Health Act (usually a consultant psychiatrist). Treatment can be given against a patient's wishes. Used for someone who will not be admitted voluntarily; patients under the influence of alcohol or drugs are specifically excluded.

title: Schizophrenia – Mental Health Act: Section 3
content: Section 3 is used for admission for treatment for up to 6 months; it can be renewed. An AMHP along with 2 doctors (both of whom must have seen the patient within the past 24 hours) make the application. Treatment can be given against a patient's wishes.

title: Schizophrenia – Mental Health Act: Sections 4, 5(2), 5(4)
content: Section 4: 72-hour assessment order used as an emergency when a Section 2 would involve unacceptable delay; requires a GP and an AMHP or NR; often changed to a Section 2 upon arrival at hospital. Section 5(2): a voluntary patient in hospital can be legally detained by a doctor for 72 hours. Section 5(4): allows a nurse to detain a voluntary patient for 6 hours.

title: Schizophrenia – Mental Health Act: Sections 17a, 135, 136
content: Section 17a (Community Treatment Order): can be used to recall a patient to hospital for treatment if they do not comply with conditions in the community. Section 135: a court order can be obtained to allow the police to break into a property to remove a person to a Place of Safety. Section 136: someone found in a public place who appears to have a mental disorder can be taken by the police to a Place of Safety; can only be used for up to 24 hours whilst a Mental Health Act assessment is arranged.

title: Somatisation – Somatisation disorder and illness anxiety disorder
content: Somatisation disorder: multiple physical symptoms present for at least 2 years; patient refuses to accept reassurance or negative test results. Illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis): persistent belief in the presence of an underlying serious disease (e.g. cancer); patient again refuses to accept reassurance or negative test results.

title: Somatisation – Functional neurological disorder and dissociative disorder
content: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder): typically involves loss of motor or sensory function; the patient does not consciously feign symptoms (factitious disorder) or seek material gain (malingering); patients may be indifferent to their apparent disorder (la belle indifférence). Dissociative disorder: dissociation is a process of 'separating off' certain memories from normal consciousness; involves psychiatric symptoms (amnesia, fugue, stupor); dissociative identity disorder (DID) is the most severe form.

title: Somatisation – Factitious disorder and malingering
content: Factitious disorder (Munchausen's syndrome): the intentional production of physical or psychological symptoms. Malingering: fraudulent simulation or exaggeration of symptoms with the intention of financial or other gain.

title: Depression – Suicide risk factors
content: Factors associated with increased risk of suicide: male sex (HR approximately 2.0); history of deliberate self-harm (HR 1.7); alcohol or drug misuse (HR 1.6); history of mental illness (depression, schizophrenia — NICE estimates 10% of people with schizophrenia will complete suicide); history of chronic disease; advancing age; unemployment or social isolation/living alone; being unmarried, divorced, or widowed.

title: Depression – Suicide risk: factors after attempted suicide
content: Factors associated with increased risk of completed suicide after an attempt: efforts to avoid discovery; planning; leaving a written note; final acts such as sorting out finances; and use of a violent method.

title: Depression – Suicide: protective factors
content: Protective factors that reduce the risk of suicide include: family support; having children at home; and religious belief.

title: Bipolar affective disorder – Hypomania vs mania: detailed comparison
content: Mania: lasts at least 7 days; causes severe functional impairment in social and work settings; may require hospitalisation due to risk of harm to self or others; may present with psychotic symptoms (delusions of grandeur, auditory hallucinations). Hypomania: a lesser version of mania; lasts <7 days (typically 3–4 days); can be high functioning and does not impair functional capacity; unlikely to require hospitalisation; does not exhibit any psychotic symptoms.
